section-98: The Constituent Assembly was formed under the Cabinet Mission Plan (1946), with members indirectly elected by provincial assemblies (292) and nominated by princely states (93), plus 4 from Chief Commissioners' provinces - 389 in total, reduced to 299 after Partition. It first met on 9 December 1946 with Dr Sachchidananda Sinha as temporary chairman; Dr Rajendra Prasad was elected permanent President (11 December 1946), and B. N. Rau was the constitutional adviser. Nehru moved the Objectives Resolution on 13 December 1946, adopted on 22 January 1947, which became the basis of the Preamble.

Important committees included the Drafting Committee (chaired by Dr B. R. Ambedkar, set up on 29 August 1947), the Union Powers and Union Constitution Committees (Nehru), the Provincial Constitution Committee and the Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights, Minorities and Tribal and Excluded Areas (Sardar Patel). The Assembly took 2 years, 11 months and 18 days, holding 11 sessions. The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949 (Constitution Day) and came into force on 26 January 1950 (Republic Day), the anniversary of the Purna Swaraj declaration of 1930.
section-99: The Preamble reads: 'We, the people of India, having solemnly resolved to constitute India into a Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic Republic and to secure to all its citizens: Justice, social, economic and political; Liberty of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship; Equality of status and of opportunity; and to promote among them all Fraternity assuring the dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the Nation; in our Constituent Assembly this twenty-sixth day of November, 1949, do hereby adopt, enact and give to ourselves this Constitution.'

The words 'Socialist', 'Secular' and 'integrity' were added by the 42nd Amendment (1976). The Preamble shows that the source of authority is the people. In the Berubari case (1960), the Supreme Court said the Preamble is not part of the Constitution, but in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) it held that the Preamble is part of the Constitution and can be amended, though not in a way that destroys the basic structure. K. M. Munshi called it the 'political horoscope' of the Constitution, and Ernest Barker called it the 'key-note'.
section-100: Fundamental Rights are in Part III (Articles 12-35), called the 'Magna Carta of India'. Originally seven, there are now six: (1) Right to Equality (Articles 14-18); (2) Right to Freedom (Articles 19-22), including six freedoms under Article 19 - speech and expression, assembly, association, movement, residence and profession - and protection of life and personal liberty (Article 21); (3) Right against Exploitation (Articles 23-24); (4) Right to Freedom of Religion (Articles 25-28); (5) Cultural and Educational Rights (Articles 29-30); and (6) Right to Constitutional Remedies (Article 32). The Right to Property (Article 31) was removed by the 44th Amendment (1978).

Features: they are justiciable (enforceable through courts), not absolute (subject to reasonable restrictions), some are available only to citizens (Articles 15, 16, 19, 29, 30) and others to all persons, and they can be suspended during a national emergency (except Articles 20 and 21, after the 44th Amendment). The Supreme Court has expanded Article 21 to include rights such as livelihood, privacy (K. S. Puttaswamy, 2017), clean environment, education, shelter and speedy trial (Maneka Gandhi case, 1978, introduced 'due process' reasoning).
section-101: Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP) are in Part IV (Articles 36-51), borrowed from the Irish Constitution. Article 37 says they are not enforceable by any court but are 'fundamental in the governance of the country', and it is the duty of the state to apply them in making laws. Ambedkar called them 'novel features' of the Constitution; Granville Austin described them, with Fundamental Rights, as the 'conscience of the Constitution'.

They can be classified as: socialist principles (Article 38 - social order based on justice; Article 39 - adequate livelihood, equitable distribution of resources, equal pay for equal work; Article 41 - right to work, education and public assistance; Article 42 - humane conditions of work and maternity relief; Article 43 - living wage); Gandhian principles (Article 40 - village panchayats; Article 43 - cottage industries; Article 46 - promotion of interests of SCs, STs and weaker sections; Article 47 - prohibition of intoxicating drinks; Article 48 - prohibition of cow slaughter); and liberal-intellectual principles (Article 44 - uniform civil code; Article 45 - early childhood care; Article 48A - environment; Article 50 - separation of judiciary from executive; Article 51 - international peace). In Minerva Mills (1980), the Supreme Court held that harmony and balance between Fundamental Rights and DPSP is part of the basic structure.
section-102: Fundamental Duties were added by the 42nd Amendment (1976) on the recommendation of the Swaran Singh Committee, as Part IVA, Article 51A, inspired by the Constitution of the former USSR. Originally ten, an eleventh was added by the 86th Amendment (2002). They include: to abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals, the National Flag and the National Anthem; to cherish the ideals of the freedom struggle; to uphold the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India; to defend the country; to promote harmony and renounce practices derogatory to the dignity of women; to preserve the composite culture; to protect the environment; to develop scientific temper and the spirit of inquiry; to safeguard public property and abjure violence; to strive for excellence; and for parents or guardians to provide educational opportunities to children aged 6 to 14.

They are not directly enforceable by courts but can be enforced through laws (such as the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971) and help courts interpret laws. They remind citizens that rights and duties go together. The Verma Committee (1999) suggested ways to make them operational.
section-103: The President (Articles 52-62) is elected indirectly by an electoral college of the elected members of both Houses of Parliament and the elected members of the state legislative assemblies (including Delhi and Puducherry), by proportional representation through the single transferable vote and secret ballot (Article 55 ensures parity between the Union and the states). The term is five years; the President can be re-elected. Qualifications: a citizen of India, at least 35 years old, qualified to be a member of the Lok Sabha and not holding an office of profit. The President can be removed by impeachment for violation of the Constitution (Article 61).

Powers: executive (appointment of the Prime Minister, ministers, Governors, judges, the CAG, Election Commissioners), legislative (summoning and proroguing Parliament, dissolving the Lok Sabha, assent to bills, ordinances under Article 123), financial (money bills require recommendation), judicial (pardon under Article 72), military (Supreme Commander) and emergency powers (Articles 352, 356, 360). The 42nd (1976) and 44th (1978) Amendments made the advice of the Council of Ministers binding, though the President may return it once for reconsideration (Article 74). Discretion exists in situations such as a hung Parliament and the 'pocket veto'. Droupadi Murmu became the 15th President in 2022.
section-104: The Prime Minister is appointed by the President (Article 75); by convention, the President appoints the leader of the majority party or coalition in the Lok Sabha. The PM must be a member of Parliament or become one within six months. The PM's term is not fixed; they hold office as long as they enjoy the confidence of the Lok Sabha.

Powers and functions: forms the Council of Ministers and allocates portfolios; presides over Cabinet meetings; coordinates government policies; is the chief link between the President and the Council of Ministers (Article 78); is the leader of the Lok Sabha (if a member); advises the President on dissolving the Lok Sabha; chairs NITI Aayog, the National Development Council and other bodies; and represents India internationally. The PM is described as 'first among equals' (primus inter pares), but in practice is the keystone of the cabinet arch; the position's strength depends on party majority and personality (Nehru, Indira Gandhi, Narendra Modi with strong majorities; coalition PMs with weaker positions).
section-105: The Council of Ministers (Article 74 and 75) includes three categories: Cabinet Ministers (senior ministers heading major departments), Ministers of State (with independent charge or assisting Cabinet ministers) and Deputy Ministers. The Cabinet is the smaller, more powerful core that makes major decisions. The 91st Amendment (2003) limited the size of the Council of Ministers to 15 percent of the total strength of the Lok Sabha.

Principles of working: collective responsibility to the Lok Sabha (Article 75(3)) - the ministry stands or falls together, and a vote of no confidence forces its resignation; individual responsibility to the President (ministers hold office during the President's pleasure, on the PM's advice); and the secrecy of cabinet proceedings (oath of secrecy). The Council of Ministers exercises the real executive power in India's parliamentary system.
section-106: Parliament (Articles 79-122) consists of the President, the Lok Sabha (House of the People) and the Rajya Sabha (Council of States). It is a bicameral legislature. Functions: legislative (making laws on Union and Concurrent List subjects, and on State List subjects in certain circumstances); financial (passing the budget, approving taxes and expenditure); control over the executive (question hour, zero hour, adjournment motions, calling attention motions, no-confidence motions, parliamentary committees such as the Public Accounts Committee); constituent (amending the Constitution under Article 368); electoral (electing the President and Vice-President); and judicial (impeachment of the President, removal of judges).

Sessions: the President summons Parliament at least twice a year with a gap of not more than six months; normally there are three sessions (Budget, Monsoon and Winter). Joint sittings (Article 108) are held to resolve deadlocks on ordinary bills; they have occurred three times (1961, 1978, 2002). A new Parliament building was inaugurated in 2023.
section-107: The Lok Sabha has a maximum strength of 552 under the Constitution (currently 543 elected members; the two nominated Anglo-Indian seats were abolished by the 104th Amendment, 2019). Members are directly elected from territorial constituencies by universal adult franchise for five years, unless dissolved earlier. Seats are reserved for SCs (84) and STs (47); the Women's Reservation Act (106th Amendment, 2023) provides for one-third reservation for women after the next census and delimitation. Qualifications: citizen, at least 25 years old. The Speaker presides; the first Speaker was G. V. Mavalankar.

Special powers of the Lok Sabha: money bills can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha (Article 110), and the Rajya Sabha can only delay them for 14 days; the Speaker certifies whether a bill is a money bill; the Council of Ministers is responsible to the Lok Sabha, which alone can pass a no-confidence motion; and in a joint sitting the Lok Sabha's larger numbers usually prevail. Mizoram elects one member to the Lok Sabha.
section-108: The Rajya Sabha has a maximum strength of 250 - 238 representatives of states and Union Territories elected by elected members of state assemblies through proportional representation by single transferable vote, and 12 members nominated by the President for expertise in literature, science, art and social service. At present it has 245 members. It is a permanent House that cannot be dissolved; one-third of members retire every two years, and members serve six-year terms. The Vice-President is the ex officio Chairman.

Seats are allotted to states according to population (Fourth Schedule): Uttar Pradesh has 31, while Mizoram and other small states have one each. Special powers: under Article 249, it can authorise Parliament to make laws on a State List subject in the national interest by a two-thirds majority; under Article 312, it can authorise the creation of new All-India Services. It acts as a revising chamber, represents the federal principle and provides a place for experienced people. Critics point to its weaker powers on money bills and the election of members from outside the states they represent.
section-109: The Supreme Court (Articles 124-147) was established on 28 January 1950. It consists of the Chief Justice of India and other judges (originally 7, now a maximum of 33 plus the CJI, total 34, since 2019). Judges are appointed by the President after consultation; the 'collegium system' (developed by the Second Judges Case, 1993, and Third Judges Case, 1998) gives a collegium of the CJI and four senior judges the decisive role. The National Judicial Appointments Commission Act (99th Amendment, 2014) was struck down in 2015. Judges retire at 65 and can be removed only by Parliament through a special majority on grounds of proved misbehaviour or incapacity.

Jurisdiction: original (disputes between the Union and states, Article 131), writ jurisdiction (Article 32 - enforcement of Fundamental Rights through habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari and quo warranto), appellate (constitutional, civil and criminal appeals, special leave petitions under Article 136), advisory (Article 143), and as a court of record (Article 129, power to punish for contempt). It is the guardian of the Constitution and protector of Fundamental Rights. Public Interest Litigation (PIL), introduced in the late 1970s and 1980s by Justices P. N. Bhagwati and V. R. Krishna Iyer, expanded access to justice.
section-110: Judicial review originated in the USA in Marbury v. Madison (1803), when Chief Justice John Marshall declared that courts could strike down laws contrary to the Constitution. In India, it is based on Articles 13 (laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights are void), 32, 226 (High Courts' writ jurisdiction) and 368. Courts can review legislative acts, executive actions and even constitutional amendments.

Important cases: Shankari Prasad (1951) and Sajjan Singh (1965) allowed amendment of Fundamental Rights; Golak Nath (1967) said Parliament cannot amend Fundamental Rights; Kesavananda Bharati (1973) established the 'basic structure doctrine' - Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution but cannot destroy its basic structure (including supremacy of the Constitution, democracy, secularism, federalism, separation of powers, judicial review and the rule of law); Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975), Minerva Mills (1980) and S. R. Bommai (1994) reinforced it. The Ninth Schedule laws were made subject to review in I. R. Coelho (2007). Judicial review is itself part of the basic structure. Critics warn of 'judicial overreach' and 'judicial activism', while supporters say it protects rights and constitutional values.
section-111: The Constitution describes India as a 'Union of States' (Article 1), not a federation. Federal features: a written and rigid constitution, division of powers through three lists in the Seventh Schedule (Union List - originally 97 subjects, now 98; State List - originally 66, now 59; Concurrent List - originally 47, now 52), an independent judiciary to settle disputes, a bicameral legislature with the Rajya Sabha representing states, and supremacy of the Constitution.

Unitary features: a strong Centre, residuary powers with the Union (Article 248), single citizenship, single constitution (except Jammu and Kashmir until 2019), integrated judiciary, All-India Services, appointment of Governors by the Centre, emergency provisions, Parliament's power to change state boundaries (Article 3), and the Centre's power to legislate on state subjects in certain conditions (Articles 249, 250, 252, 253). K. C. Wheare called India 'quasi-federal'; Ivor Jennings called it 'a federation with a strong centralising tendency'; Granville Austin called it 'cooperative federalism'; and the Supreme Court in S. R. Bommai (1994) declared federalism a basic feature. Recent terms include 'competitive federalism' and 'cooperative federalism' (NITI Aayog, GST Council).
section-112: Legislative relations (Articles 245-255): Parliament can make laws for the whole or any part of India; states for their own territory. Subjects are divided into the three lists. Parliament can legislate on State List subjects when the Rajya Sabha passes a resolution (Article 249), during an emergency (Article 250), when two or more states request (Article 252), to implement international treaties (Article 253), and under President's Rule. In conflicts on Concurrent subjects, Union law prevails (Article 254). Governors can reserve state bills for the President's consideration (Article 200-201).

Administrative relations (Articles 256-263): states must comply with Union laws; the Centre can give directions to states; All-India Services; the Inter-State Council (Article 263, set up in 1990); Governors as agents of the Centre; and Article 356 (President's Rule), used over 100 times, often misused before the Bommai judgement (1994). Financial relations (Articles 264-293): division of taxing powers; the Finance Commission (Article 280) recommends sharing of central taxes and grants; the GST (101st Amendment, 2016) created the GST Council. Commissions on Centre-State relations include the Administrative Reforms Commission (1966), the Rajamannar Committee (Tamil Nadu, 1969), the Sarkaria Commission (1983-1988) and the Punchhi Commission (2007-2010). Issues include the misuse of Article 356, the role of Governors, financial dependence and demands for greater autonomy.
section-113: The Election Commission of India (Article 324), established on 25 January 1950 (National Voters' Day), superintends, directs and controls the preparation of electoral rolls and the conduct of elections to Parliament, state legislatures and the offices of President and Vice-President. Since 1993, it has been a three-member body consisting of a Chief Election Commissioner and two Election Commissioners. The CEC can be removed only like a Supreme Court judge. Sukumar Sen was the first CEC. T. N. Seshan (1990-1996) strictly enforced the Model Code of Conduct.

Functions: delimitation-related work, preparation and revision of electoral rolls, issuing voter ID cards (EPIC), recognising political parties and allotting symbols, scheduling elections, enforcing the Model Code of Conduct, supervising election expenditure, deciding disputes on symbols, and conducting elections using Electronic Voting Machines (EVMs, used nationwide since 2004) and VVPAT. Issues include money power, criminalisation, paid news, misuse of social media and debates about the appointment process (the 2023 Act on appointment of Election Commissioners). State Election Commissions (Articles 243K and 243ZA) conduct local body elections.
section-114: The Election Commission recognises parties as national or state parties based on criteria such as the percentage of votes and seats won in Lok Sabha or Assembly elections (a national party must, for example, win at least 6 percent of votes in four or more states and four Lok Sabha seats, or 2 percent of Lok Sabha seats from at least three states, or be a recognised state party in four states). As of 2023, there are six national parties: the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), the Indian National Congress (INC), the Communist Party of India (Marxist), the Bahujan Samaj Party (BSP), the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) and the National People's Party (NPP) of Meghalaya.

The party system has evolved through phases: one-party dominance of the Congress ('Congress system', Rajni Kothari, 1952-1967); the decline of Congress and the rise of opposition and regional parties (1967-1989, with the Janata government of 1977); the era of coalitions (1989-2014 - National Front, United Front, NDA, UPA); and BJP dominance since 2014. Regional parties include the DMK, AIADMK, TMC, Shiv Sena, TDP, BJD, SP, RJD, JD(U) and MNF and ZPM in Mizoram. Issues include lack of internal democracy, dynastic politics, defections and funding (the electoral bond scheme was struck down by the Supreme Court in 2024).
section-115: Rajni Kothari ('Caste in Indian Politics', 1970) argued that caste has been 'politicised' and politics 'casteised': caste groups are mobilised for votes, parties select candidates according to the caste composition of constituencies, and caste associations act as pressure groups. Lloyd and Susanne Rudolph described the 'modernity of tradition', in which caste associations became vehicles of democratic participation.

Caste-based mobilisation includes the rise of OBC politics after the Mandal Commission (1980, implemented 1990, with 27 percent reservation for OBCs), Dalit parties such as the BSP (Kanshi Ram, Mayawati), parties based on caste coalitions (the SP, RJD), and caste census debates (Bihar's caste survey of 2023). Reservations in legislatures, jobs and education for SCs and STs (Articles 15(4), 16(4), 330, 332) have increased representation. Effects: positive (empowerment of marginalised groups, wider participation) and negative (vote-bank politics, conflicts between castes, neglect of merit and development issues).
section-116: Indian secularism, as described in the Constitution (Articles 25-28 and the Preamble), means that the state has no official religion, treats all religions equally (sarva dharma sambhava), guarantees freedom of religion to all and does not discriminate on religious grounds. Unlike the Western model of strict separation of church and state, Indian secularism allows state intervention in religious matters for social reform (for example, temple entry laws, abolition of untouchability and regulation of religious institutions) - Rajeev Bhargava calls it 'principled distance'.

Religion has influenced politics through communal parties, riots (Partition, 1984 anti-Sikh riots, Babri Masjid demolition 1992, Gujarat 2002), debates on the Uniform Civil Code, the Shah Bano case (1985), the Ram Janmabhoomi movement and the Supreme Court's Ayodhya judgement (2019), the Citizenship Amendment Act (2019) and the rise of Hindutva politics. Critics argue that some parties practise 'vote-bank' politics or majoritarianism. The Supreme Court in S. R. Bommai (1994) held secularism to be part of the basic structure.
section-117: Regionalism is loyalty to a particular region and the demand for its interests, identity and autonomy. Causes include linguistic and cultural identity, uneven economic development, historical factors, geographical isolation, the neglect of regions by the Centre, sons-of-the-soil feelings and the role of regional parties. Forms include demands for separate states (Telangana, created in 2014; Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh and Uttarakhand, created in 2000), greater autonomy (Tamil Nadu's DMK, Punjab's Anandpur Sahib Resolution, 1973), inter-state disputes (water - Kaveri; boundaries - Assam-Mizoram), and secessionism (insurgencies in the Northeast, Khalistan, Kashmir).

The States Reorganisation Commission (Fazl Ali, 1953-1955) led to the reorganisation of states on linguistic lines (1956), after the death of Potti Sriramulu fasting for Andhra (1952). Regionalism can be positive - promoting regional development, culture and federal balance - or negative, threatening national unity when it becomes separatist or chauvinistic (anti-migrant movements). Responses include federalism, special provisions (Articles 371-371J), autonomous councils and balanced development.
section-118: A coalition government is formed when two or more parties combine because no single party has a majority. Coalitions may be pre-poll (alliances before elections) or post-poll. In India, coalition politics began at the state level in 1967 (the Samyukta Vidhayak Dal governments) and at the Centre with the Janata Party government (1977-1979). From 1989 to 2014, no single party won a majority in the Lok Sabha: the National Front (V. P. Singh, 1989), the United Front (1996-1998), the NDA under Atal Bihari Vajpayee (1998-2004) and the UPA under Manmohan Singh (2004-2014) were coalitions.

Advantages: wider representation of regional and social groups, consensus-based decision-making and checks on the dominance of one party. Disadvantages: instability (governments falling due to withdrawal of support), policy paralysis, bargaining and 'coalition dharma' compromises, and disproportionate influence of small parties. Coalitions use mechanisms such as a Common Minimum Programme and coordination committees. Even after 2014, the BJP governs with NDA allies, and after the 2024 elections, the BJP needed allies (TDP, JD(U)) to form a majority.
section-120: Making of the Constitution: the Constituent Assembly (1946-1949), with Rajendra Prasad as President and Ambedkar as Chairman of the Drafting Committee; the Objectives Resolution (1946); adoption on 26 November 1949; commencement on 26 January 1950. Sources: the Government of India Act 1935 (federal scheme, emergency provisions, Governor's office), British Constitution (parliamentary government, rule of law, single citizenship), US Constitution (Fundamental Rights, judicial review, independent judiciary, impeachment), Irish Constitution (DPSP, nomination to Rajya Sabha), Canada (strong Centre), Australia (Concurrent List), Weimar Germany (suspension of rights in emergency), USSR (Fundamental Duties) and France (republic, liberty, equality, fraternity).

Salient features: lengthiest written constitution; blend of rigidity and flexibility; parliamentary form of government; federal system with unitary bias; Fundamental Rights, DPSP and Fundamental Duties; independent and integrated judiciary; universal adult franchise; secular state; single citizenship; emergency provisions; independent bodies (Election Commission, CAG, UPSC); three-tier government (panchayats and municipalities after 1992); and special provisions for SCs, STs and certain states.

Preamble: sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic republic; justice, liberty, equality and fraternity. Rights, DPSP and Duties together express political democracy (rights), social and economic democracy (DPSP) and civic responsibility (duties). The Constitution is a 'living document' that has been amended over 100 times, guided by the basic structure doctrine.
section-121: President: the constitutional head, elected indirectly for five years; executive, legislative, financial, judicial, military and emergency powers; acts on the advice of the Council of Ministers (Article 74), with limited discretion (appointment of the PM in a hung Parliament, returning advice once, pocket veto). The Vice-President is the ex officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha and acts as President when needed.

Prime Minister and Council of Ministers: the real executive; the PM is appointed by the President as leader of the majority in the Lok Sabha, forms the ministry, presides over the Cabinet, coordinates policy and leads the nation; the Council of Ministers (limited to 15 percent of Lok Sabha strength) is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha. Parliament: the President, Lok Sabha (543 elected, five-year term, directly elected, controls money bills and confidence) and Rajya Sabha (245, permanent house, represents states).

Executive-legislature relations: the executive is drawn from and responsible to the legislature; Parliament controls the executive through questions, debates, motions, committees and financial control; the executive leads the legislature through party majority and initiative in legislation. With strong majorities, the executive dominates ('cabinet dictatorship'); with coalitions, Parliament is more influential. Declining sittings, disruptions and frequent use of ordinances are concerns about the functioning of Parliament.
section-122: Organisation: the Chief Justice of India and up to 33 other judges; appointed by the President through the collegium system; retirement at 65; removal only by Parliament through a special majority. Independence is secured by security of tenure, fixed salaries charged on the Consolidated Fund, prohibition of practice after retirement, power to punish for contempt, and separation from the executive (Article 50).

Jurisdiction: original, writ (Article 32 - Ambedkar called it 'the heart and soul of the Constitution'), appellate, advisory (Article 143) and court of record (Article 129). Judicial review allows the Court to declare laws and executive actions unconstitutional; the basic structure doctrine (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973) limits Parliament's amending power. Judicial activism through PIL has addressed issues such as bonded labour, prisoners' rights, environment (M. C. Mehta cases), sexual harassment (Vishaka, 1997) and the right to food.

Evaluation: the Supreme Court has protected Fundamental Rights, upheld federalism (Bommai), secularism and the rule of law, and expanded Article 21. Criticisms include pendency of cases (over 80,000 in the Supreme Court and millions in lower courts), the opacity of the collegium system, judicial overreach into policy matters and delays. The judiciary is nevertheless central to maintaining constitutional supremacy and limiting arbitrary government.
section-123: Nature of Indian federalism: federal features (written constitution, division of powers, independent judiciary, bicameralism) combined with unitary features (strong Centre, residuary powers, single citizenship, All-India Services, Governors, emergency powers, Parliament's power to reorganise states). Scholars describe it as quasi-federal (Wheare), cooperative (Austin), bargaining federalism (Morris-Jones) or asymmetrical federalism (special provisions for certain states under Articles 371A-371J, Sixth Schedule areas).

Centre-State relations: legislative (three lists and Union supremacy in conflicts), administrative (directions to states, Governors, All-India Services, Article 356) and financial (division of taxes, Finance Commission, grants, GST Council). Tensions have arisen over the misuse of Article 356 (before Bommai, 1994), the role and appointment of Governors, delays in assent to state bills (the Supreme Court in 2023-2024 set limits on such delays), financial dependence, central agencies and the control of police and resources.

Political factors: the dominance of the Congress until 1967 kept tensions low; the rise of regional parties and coalitions increased states' bargaining power; and since 2014 strong central governments have again centralised power, while also promoting 'cooperative federalism' (NITI Aayog replacing the Planning Commission, 2015; GST). Commissions (Sarkaria, Punchhi) recommended greater consultation and restraint in using Article 356. Indian federalism is thus shaped by both the Constitution and political practice.
section-124: Political parties and elections: India has a multi-party system with national and regional parties; the party system has evolved from Congress dominance to coalitions to BJP dominance. Elections are conducted by the Election Commission through universal adult franchise, the first-past-the-post system and EVMs. Indian elections are the largest in the world (about 97 crore voters in 2024). Problems include money power, criminalisation, defections, misuse of government machinery and fake news; reforms include the Model Code of Conduct, expenditure limits, NOTA (2013), disclosure of criminal records and the anti-defection law.

Social factors: caste is mobilised in elections and through reservations; religion shapes identity politics and debates on secularism; regionalism leads to demands for states, autonomy and regional parties; language, tribe and class also influence politics. Coalition politics (1989-2014) gave regional parties an important role at the Centre.

Evaluation: Indian democracy has deepened through high voter turnout (especially among women and the poor), peaceful transfers of power and the rise of marginalised groups (Yogendra Yadav's 'second democratic upsurge'). At the same time, challenges remain: communal polarisation, caste conflict, criminalisation, the weakening of institutions and inequality. Indian democracy thus works through both constitutional institutions and complex social forces.
section-127: Comparative politics studies political systems, institutions and processes across countries to find similarities, differences and general patterns. Aristotle compared 158 Greek constitutions; Montesquieu, Tocqueville ('Democracy in America', 1835-1840) and Bryce ('Modern Democracies', 1921) continued the tradition. The traditional approach focused on formal institutions and constitutions, mainly of Western countries.

After the Second World War, the modern approach (Gabriel Almond, Sidney Verba, David Easton, Lucian Pye) broadened the scope to include developing countries, political culture ('The Civic Culture', Almond and Verba, 1963), political development, political socialisation and behaviour, using methods such as systems analysis and structural-functionalism. Comparative politics helps us understand why democracies succeed or fail, the effects of electoral systems and federalism, and lessons from other countries' experiences. Methods include case studies, comparisons of few cases and statistical comparisons of many countries.
section-128: David Easton ('The Political System', 1953; 'A Systems Analysis of Political Life', 1965) defined the political system as the set of interactions through which values are authoritatively allocated for a society. It receives inputs (demands and supports) from the environment, converts them through institutions into outputs (decisions and policies), which produce feedback that affects new inputs. The system tries to maintain itself in a changing environment.

Gabriel Almond's structural-functional approach identified input functions (political socialisation and recruitment, interest articulation, interest aggregation, political communication) and output functions (rule-making, rule application and rule adjudication), performed by structures such as parties, pressure groups, legislatures, executives and courts. The political system is broader than the state, including informal institutions and behaviour. Critics argue that systems analysis is too abstract and conservative, emphasising stability over change.
section-129: The parliamentary system originated in Britain and is also called cabinet or responsible government. Features: a nominal or titular head of state (monarch or president) and a real executive (the Prime Minister and Cabinet); the executive is drawn from the legislature; collective responsibility of the cabinet to the lower house; the government can be removed by a vote of no confidence; the leadership of the Prime Minister; dissolution of the lower house before its term; and fusion of powers between executive and legislature. Countries include Britain, India, Canada, Australia, Japan and Germany.

Merits: harmony between executive and legislature, responsible government, flexibility (governments can be changed without waiting for elections), and representation of diverse groups in the cabinet. Demerits: instability in coalitions or with weak majorities, cabinet dictatorship with strong majorities, violation of the separation of powers and a temptation to place party interests over national interest. Walter Bagehot ('The English Constitution', 1867) described the cabinet as 'a hyphen which joins, a buckle which fastens, the legislative part of the state to the executive part'.
section-130: The presidential system is best illustrated by the USA. Features: the President is both head of state and head of government; elected (directly or through an electoral college) for a fixed term (four years in the USA, maximum two terms by the 22nd Amendment, 1951); the President and cabinet secretaries are not members of the legislature; the President is not responsible to the legislature and cannot be removed by a no-confidence vote (only by impeachment); the legislature cannot be dissolved by the President; and there is separation of powers with checks and balances. Other examples include Brazil, Mexico, Indonesia and the Philippines; France and Russia have semi-presidential systems.

Merits: stability (fixed terms), strong leadership, separation of powers that protects liberty, and the ability to appoint experts to the cabinet. Demerits: possibility of deadlock between the executive and legislature (especially in 'divided government', when different parties control the presidency and Congress), rigidity (difficult to remove an incompetent president), and danger of authoritarianism in some countries. Juan Linz ('The Perils of Presidentialism', 1990) argued that parliamentary systems are more stable for new democracies.
section-131: Britain has no single written constitution. Its sources include: historical charters and statutes (Magna Carta 1215, the Petition of Right 1628, the Bill of Rights 1689, the Act of Settlement 1701, the Parliament Acts of 1911 and 1949, the Human Rights Act 1998, the Constitutional Reform Act 2005, the Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland devolution acts of 1998), judicial decisions (common law), conventions, and works of authority (Dicey, Bagehot, Erskine May). The UK's membership of the European Union (1973-2020) also affected its constitution until Brexit.

Features: unwritten (uncodified) and flexible - any law can be changed by an ordinary Act of Parliament; parliamentary sovereignty - Parliament can make or unmake any law, and no court can strike down an Act of Parliament; constitutional monarchy - the monarch reigns but does not rule; unitary state with devolution; rule of law; parliamentary government; bicameral Parliament; and an independent judiciary (the Supreme Court of the UK was created in 2009, replacing the Law Lords of the House of Lords). Britain is called the 'mother of parliaments'.
section-132: A. V. Dicey explained the rule of law as a key feature of the British constitution: (1) absence of arbitrary power - no one can be punished except for a breach of law proved before ordinary courts; (2) equality before the law - every person, whatever their rank, is subject to the ordinary law and the jurisdiction of ordinary courts; there is no separate administrative law for officials (as in France's 'droit administratif'); (3) the general principles of the constitution, such as personal liberty and freedom of assembly, are the result of judicial decisions in particular cases, rather than being derived from a written constitution.

Criticism: Dicey's description was not fully accurate even in his time, since officials enjoyed special powers and immunities, and the growth of the welfare state led to delegated legislation and administrative tribunals. Lord Bingham ('The Rule of Law', 2010) offered a broader modern definition, including accessibility of law, equality, human rights, fair trial and compliance with international law. The rule of law remains a core principle of British and Indian constitutional government.
section-133: Conventions are unwritten rules of political behaviour that are generally followed, though they are not enforced by courts. Dicey called them 'rules for determining the mode in which the discretionary powers of the Crown ought to be exercised'. Examples: the monarch gives royal assent to bills passed by Parliament (the last refusal was in 1708 by Queen Anne); the monarch appoints the leader of the majority party in the House of Commons as Prime Minister; the Prime Minister must be a member of the House of Commons; the cabinet is collectively responsible to the Commons; a government defeated on a vote of confidence must resign or call an election; the monarch acts on the advice of ministers; and the House of Lords does not reject the government's manifesto bills (the Salisbury Convention).

Conventions are obeyed because breaking them would cause political crisis, public criticism or legal changes, and because they reflect democratic principles. They make the British constitution flexible. India has also adopted many conventions, such as appointing the leader of the majority party as Prime Minister.
section-134: The British Parliament, at Westminster, consists of the Crown (the monarch, currently King Charles III since 2022), the House of Lords (upper house) and the House of Commons (lower house). Legislation requires the approval of both houses and the royal assent (except under the Parliament Acts). Parliament is sovereign: it can make or repeal any law; no Parliament can bind its successors; and no court can declare an Act invalid.

Functions: making laws; controlling finance (budget and taxes); scrutinising the government through Question Time (including Prime Minister's Questions), debates, select committees and no-confidence motions; representing the people; and making and breaking governments. The Speaker of the House of Commons is impartial and leaves their party on election; by convention, the Speaker is re-elected unopposed by major parties.
section-135: The House of Commons has 650 members (MPs) elected from single-member constituencies by the first-past-the-post system, for a maximum term of five years (the Fixed-term Parliaments Act 2011 was repealed in 2022, restoring the Prime Minister's power to request dissolution). The government is formed by the party commanding a majority; the second-largest party forms 'His Majesty's Most Loyal Opposition', with a 'shadow cabinet'.

The Commons is the dominant house: money bills must originate there and the Lords cannot delay them for more than one month (Parliament Act 1911); the Lords can delay other bills for only one year (Parliament Act 1949); the government is responsible to the Commons, which can force its resignation through a vote of no confidence (as in 1979, when James Callaghan's government lost by one vote). The Commons is thus the centre of British democracy.
section-136: The House of Lords is not elected. Its members include life peers (appointed by the monarch on the advice of the Prime Minister, under the Life Peerages Act 1958 - the majority), 92 hereditary peers (after the House of Lords Act 1999 removed most hereditary peers), and 26 Lords Spiritual (bishops of the Church of England). Its size is around 800, making it one of the largest legislative chambers. Until 2009, the Law Lords served as the highest court of appeal; this role was transferred to the Supreme Court.

Functions: revising and scrutinising legislation, proposing amendments, delaying bills (up to one year), debating issues, and scrutinising government through committees with expert members. Its powers are limited by the Parliament Acts of 1911 and 1949 and the Salisbury Convention. Debate continues on reform - whether it should be elected, reduced in size or abolished - because an unelected chamber seems undemocratic, though supporters value the expertise and independence of its members.
section-137: The office developed in the eighteenth century, with Sir Robert Walpole (1721-1742) regarded as the first Prime Minister. The monarch appoints the leader of the majority party in the House of Commons, by convention, and the PM must be a member of the Commons. The PM's official residence is 10 Downing Street.

Powers: selects and dismisses ministers; chairs the Cabinet; controls the agenda and Cabinet committees; leads the majority party; advises the monarch on appointments (peers, bishops, senior officials) and dissolution; leads foreign and defence policy; and represents Britain abroad. Descriptions range from 'first among equals' to 'elected monarch' and 'prime ministerial government' (Richard Crossman). The PM's power depends on the party's majority and popularity - strong PMs such as Margaret Thatcher and Tony Blair, while others (Theresa May, Liz Truss, who served only 49 days in 2022) were weakened by party divisions. Keir Starmer became Prime Minister after the Labour victory in July 2024.
section-138: The Cabinet consists of about 20-25 senior ministers chosen by the Prime Minister from the majority party, usually from the House of Commons, with a few from the Lords. Key members include the Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance), the Foreign Secretary and the Home Secretary. The Cabinet determines government policy, controls the executive departments, initiates legislation and coordinates administration. It works through Cabinet committees and the Cabinet Office.

Principles: collective responsibility (ministers must publicly support Cabinet decisions or resign), individual ministerial responsibility for their departments, confidentiality of proceedings, and the leadership of the PM. Bagehot called the Cabinet the 'efficient secret' of the English constitution. With a strong majority, the Cabinet dominates Parliament - Lord Hailsham called this 'elective dictatorship'. The 'shadow cabinet' of the opposition presents alternative policies.
section-139: The US Constitution was drafted at the Philadelphia Convention (1787) under George Washington's presidency, with James Madison called the 'father of the Constitution'; it came into force in 1789. It is the oldest written national constitution still in use, and very brief, with only seven articles. It has been amended only 27 times; the first ten amendments (1791) form the Bill of Rights. Amendment requires a two-thirds majority of both houses of Congress and ratification by three-fourths of states, making it very rigid.

Features: written and rigid; federal (power divided between national and state governments); presidential system; separation of powers (Article I - Congress; Article II - President; Article III - judiciary) with checks and balances; judicial review; Bill of Rights; republicanism; and popular sovereignty ('We the People'). The Federalist Papers (Madison, Hamilton and Jay) explained and defended the Constitution. Important amendments include the 13th (abolition of slavery, 1865), 14th (equal protection, 1868), 15th (voting regardless of race), 19th (women's suffrage, 1920) and 26th (voting age 18, 1971).
section-140: The US President is elected for four years through the Electoral College (538 electors; a candidate needs 270), with each state having electors equal to its members of Congress; most states give all their electors to the winner of the state's popular vote, so a candidate can win the presidency while losing the national popular vote (as in 2000 and 2016). Qualifications: natural-born citizen, at least 35 years old, resident for 14 years. The 22nd Amendment (1951) limits presidents to two terms.

Powers: chief executive (enforces laws, appoints officials and judges with the Senate's consent, issues executive orders); commander-in-chief of the armed forces; chief diplomat (makes treaties with the Senate's two-thirds approval, receives ambassadors); legislative role (State of the Union address, veto power - Congress can override by a two-thirds majority in both houses; 'pocket veto'); and judicial (pardons). Checks: Congress controls funds and can impeach (the House impeaches, the Senate tries; three presidents - Andrew Johnson, Bill Clinton and Donald Trump (twice) - were impeached but none was convicted; Nixon resigned in 1974). The President has become very powerful, described by Arthur Schlesinger as the 'Imperial Presidency'.
section-141: Congress (Article I) is bicameral. The House of Representatives has 435 members elected for two years from districts allocated according to population; the Speaker presides and is a powerful party leader. The Senate has 100 members (two from each state, regardless of population) elected for six years, with one-third elected every two years; the Vice-President presides. This compromise (the 'Great Compromise' or Connecticut Compromise of 1787) balanced the interests of large and small states.

Powers: making laws (both houses must pass bills), levying taxes and appropriating funds ('power of the purse'; revenue bills must originate in the House), declaring war, regulating commerce, approving appointments and treaties (Senate), impeachment (House impeaches, Senate tries) and overriding presidential vetoes (two-thirds of both houses). The Senate is considered one of the most powerful upper houses in the world. Committees play a central role in legislation. The 'filibuster' (prolonged debate) in the Senate can block bills unless 60 senators vote to end it.
section-142: The US Supreme Court (Article III) has nine justices, including the Chief Justice, appointed by the President with the Senate's consent and serving for life ('during good behaviour'). It has original jurisdiction in limited cases (involving states and ambassadors) and appellate jurisdiction, selecting about 60-80 cases a year from thousands of petitions (writ of certiorari).

Its power of judicial review, established in Marbury v. Madison (1803), makes it the final interpreter of the Constitution. Landmark decisions: Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857, upholding slavery), Plessy v. Ferguson (1896, 'separate but equal'), Brown v. Board of Education (1954, ending school segregation), Miranda v. Arizona (1966), Roe v. Wade (1973, abortion rights - overturned by Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization in 2022), and Obergefell v. Hodges (2015, same-sex marriage). The Court has been described as 'a continuous constitutional convention'. Debates continue about the politicisation of appointments.
section-143: Montesquieu ('The Spirit of the Laws', 1748), based on his reading of the British constitution, argued that liberty requires the separation of legislative, executive and judicial powers: 'When the legislative and executive powers are united in the same person, or in the same body of magistrates, there can be no liberty... Again, there is no liberty if the judiciary power be not separated from the legislative and executive.' Locke had earlier distinguished legislative and executive powers.

The US Constitution applies this principle most fully: Congress makes laws, the President executes them, and the courts interpret them; members of one branch cannot serve in another. In parliamentary systems (Britain, India), the executive and legislature are fused, though the judiciary is independent; India follows a 'functional separation' rather than strict separation. Critics argue that complete separation is impossible and could cause deadlock; hence it is combined with checks and balances.
section-144: Checks and balances mean that each branch has some power over the others so that no branch becomes too powerful. In the USA: Congress checks the President by overriding vetoes, controlling funds, approving appointments and treaties (Senate) and impeachment; the President checks Congress through the veto and checks the judiciary by appointing judges; the judiciary checks both through judicial review; Congress checks the judiciary by approving appointments, impeaching judges, and proposing constitutional amendments; and the people check all through elections.

Madison (Federalist No. 51) explained: 'Ambition must be made to counteract ambition.' In India, checks include judicial review, parliamentary control over the executive, presidential assent and return of bills, and the impeachment of the President and removal of judges. Checks and balances protect liberty but can also cause gridlock, as with US government shutdowns over budget disputes.
section-145: The USA was the first modern federation (1787). The Constitution lists the powers of the federal government (enumerated powers in Article I, Section 8 - defence, foreign affairs, currency, interstate commerce, post offices), while the Tenth Amendment reserves all other powers to the states or the people. Concurrent powers include taxation and borrowing. States have their own constitutions, governors, legislatures and courts, and control areas such as education, police, local government and most criminal law. The Supreme Court resolves disputes, and federal law is supreme in conflicts (Supremacy Clause, Article VI).

American federalism has evolved from 'dual federalism' (separate spheres, 'layer cake') to 'cooperative federalism' ('marble cake', especially after the New Deal of the 1930s, with federal grants to states) and 'new federalism' (returning powers to states, from Nixon and Reagan). The federal government's power has grown through the Commerce Clause and the 'necessary and proper' clause. Compared with India, US federalism is a 'holding together' of independent states that came together, with residuary powers with the states, dual citizenship and equal representation of states in the Senate.
section-146: Switzerland is a federal republic of 26 cantons, with four national languages (German, French, Italian and Romansh). Its constitution (1848, revised in 1874 and 1999) combines representative democracy with direct democracy. The executive is the Federal Council, a collegial body of seven members elected by the Federal Assembly for four years; the presidency rotates annually among its members. The Federal Assembly is bicameral: the National Council (200 members, by population) and the Council of States (46 members, two from each full canton).

Direct democratic devices include the compulsory referendum (constitutional amendments must be approved by a majority of voters and a majority of cantons - the 'double majority'), the optional referendum (50,000 citizens can demand a vote on a law passed by the Assembly within 100 days), the popular initiative (100,000 citizens can propose a constitutional amendment within 18 months), and the Landsgemeinde (open-air assemblies in Appenzell Innerrhoden and Glarus). Swiss citizens vote several times a year on national, cantonal and local issues. Women got the vote in federal elections only in 1971. Switzerland is famous for consensus politics and the 'magic formula' of sharing Federal Council seats among major parties.
section-147: A referendum (from Latin 'referre', to refer back) refers a law, constitutional amendment or policy question to the voters for approval or rejection. Types: compulsory or mandatory referendum (required by the constitution, such as constitutional amendments in Switzerland and Australia) and optional or facultative referendum (held on the demand of a certain number of citizens or government). A plebiscite is a vote on an important political question, such as independence, sovereignty or the form of government.

Examples: the UK's 2016 referendum on leaving the European Union (Brexit), the Scottish independence referendum (2014), the Irish referendums on same-sex marriage (2015) and abortion (2018), and the Junagadh plebiscite in India (1948). Merits: direct expression of popular will, legitimacy for major decisions, and political education. Demerits: complex issues reduced to yes or no, low turnout, manipulation by campaigns, and possible tyranny of the majority.
section-148: An initiative is a device by which a specified number of citizens can propose a new law or constitutional amendment, which is then put to a popular vote (direct initiative) or to the legislature first (indirect initiative). In Switzerland, 100,000 signatures collected within 18 months can propose a constitutional amendment, which then requires a double majority of voters and cantons. Many Swiss initiatives are rejected, but they force public debate; examples include initiatives on immigration (2014, approved), banning minarets (2009, approved) and a basic income (2016, rejected).

Initiatives are also used in many US states (California's propositions) and Italy (abrogative referendums). Merits: citizens can bypass an unresponsive legislature and bring new issues to the agenda. Demerits: well-funded interest groups can dominate, poorly drafted proposals can cause problems, and minority rights may be threatened. Recall, another device, allows voters to remove an elected official before the end of the term (as in some US states and Swiss cantons).
section-150: Purpose and methods: comparative politics compares political systems to understand how institutions work in different contexts, to develop general theories (for example, of democracy and development) and to learn lessons. Approaches include the traditional institutional approach (constitutions and formal institutions), systems approach (Easton), structural-functional approach (Almond), political culture (Almond and Verba), political economy and new institutionalism. Methods include case studies, comparison of similar and different systems, and statistical analysis.

Major classifications: (1) parliamentary versus presidential systems - fusion versus separation of executive and legislature, collective responsibility versus fixed term, flexibility versus stability; (2) federal versus unitary systems - division of power between national and regional governments versus concentration of power (Britain, France, Japan are unitary, though with devolution); (3) representative versus direct democracy; and (4) democratic versus authoritarian regimes.

Comparing Britain (parliamentary, unitary, uncodified constitution, parliamentary sovereignty), the USA (presidential, federal, written and rigid constitution, judicial review, separation of powers) and Switzerland (collegial executive, federal, direct democracy) shows that democracy can take various institutional forms. India combines British parliamentary government with American-style fundamental rights, judicial review and federalism, adapted to Indian conditions.
section-151: Constitution: uncodified and flexible, derived from statutes (Magna Carta, Bill of Rights, Parliament Acts, Human Rights Act), conventions, common law and authoritative works. Principles: parliamentary sovereignty (Dicey), rule of law (Dicey's three principles), constitutional monarchy, unitary state with devolution to Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland (1998), and conventions that make the system work.

Parliament: the Crown, House of Lords (life peers, 92 hereditary peers, 26 bishops; revising chamber with limited powers under the Parliament Acts 1911 and 1949) and House of Commons (650 MPs elected by FPTP; dominant chamber controlling finance and government survival). The monarch has formal powers (royal prerogative) exercised on ministerial advice. Executive: the Prime Minister (leader of the majority party in the Commons) and the Cabinet, bound by collective responsibility. The opposition and shadow cabinet provide an alternative government. The two-party system (Conservative and Labour) has dominated, though the Liberal Democrats, Scottish National Party and others have grown.

Evaluation: the British system has evolved gradually, combining tradition and democracy; it provides strong, accountable government but can lead to 'elective dictatorship' when a government has a large majority. Reforms include the Human Rights Act (1998), devolution, the Supreme Court (2009) and House of Lords reform. Brexit raised constitutional questions about parliamentary sovereignty, referendums and the union. Britain remains the classic model of parliamentary government, followed by India and many Commonwealth countries.
section-152: Constitution: written, brief (seven articles, 27 amendments) and rigid; based on popular sovereignty, federalism, separation of powers, checks and balances, judicial review and the Bill of Rights. Executive: the President, elected for four years through the Electoral College, is head of state and government, commander-in-chief and chief diplomat, with veto power, and is not responsible to Congress; the cabinet consists of secretaries appointed with the Senate's consent.

Legislature: Congress - the House of Representatives (435, two-year terms, by population) and the Senate (100, six-year terms, two per state, powers over treaties and appointments). Judiciary: the Supreme Court (nine justices, life tenure) with judicial review since Marbury v. Madison (1803). Checks and balances: vetoes and overrides, Senate approval of appointments and treaties, impeachment, the power of the purse and judicial review. Federalism: enumerated federal powers, reserved state powers (Tenth Amendment), and evolution from dual to cooperative federalism.

Evaluation: the American system protects liberty through divided power and has proved durable for over two centuries. Criticisms include gridlock when different parties control Congress and the presidency, the influence of money and lobbying in politics, the Electoral College producing presidents who lost the popular vote, and the growing polarisation of politics. Comparison with India: India borrowed judicial review and fundamental rights, but adopted a parliamentary rather than presidential executive and a centralised rather than state-centred federalism.
section-153: Swiss political system: a federal state of 26 cantons with linguistic and religious diversity; a bicameral Federal Assembly (National Council and Council of States); a collegial executive - the Federal Council of seven members elected by the Assembly, with a rotating one-year presidency and consensus-based decision-making (the 'magic formula'); and a Federal Supreme Court at Lausanne (which cannot review federal laws for constitutionality). It is often described as a 'consensus democracy' (Arend Lijphart).

Direct democracy devices: the compulsory referendum on constitutional amendments (double majority of voters and cantons); the optional referendum on federal laws (50,000 signatures within 100 days); the popular initiative for constitutional amendments (100,000 signatures within 18 months); and the Landsgemeinde in two cantons. Citizens vote several times a year on a wide range of issues, from taxes and immigration to environmental policy and EU relations (Switzerland is not an EU member and voted against joining the European Economic Area in 1992).

Evaluation: merits include direct popular control, political education, legitimacy of decisions, protection of minorities through federalism and consensus, and political stability. Limitations include low turnout in some votes (often below 50 percent), the influence of well-funded campaigns, slow decision-making, the possibility of majority decisions against minorities (such as the minaret ban), and the difficulty of applying such a system to large countries. Switzerland is a unique model of combining representative and direct democracy.
section-156: A constitution is the fundamental and supreme law of a country that establishes the structure and powers of government, the relationship between government and citizens, and fundamental rights. Kinds: written (India, USA) and unwritten (UK); rigid (USA, Australia) and flexible (UK, New Zealand); federal and unitary. A constitution reflects the values and aspirations of the people and limits government power (constitutionalism).

The Indian Constitution is the longest written constitution in the world. It has a Preamble, 25 parts, 12 schedules and about 470 articles (originally 395 articles in 22 parts and 8 schedules). It is partly rigid and partly flexible: some provisions can be amended by simple majority, others by special majority of Parliament, and some require ratification by half the states (Article 368).
section-157: The idea of a Constituent Assembly was first put forward by M. N. Roy in 1934 and adopted by the Congress in 1935; the British accepted it in the August Offer (1940) and the Cripps Mission (1942). The Assembly was elected in July 1946 under the Cabinet Mission Plan, indirectly by provincial assemblies on the basis of one seat per million population, with seats divided among Muslims, Sikhs and general communities. Princely states sent nominated representatives. The Muslim League boycotted it after the partition decision; after Partition, the Assembly had 299 members, including 15 women (such as Sarojini Naidu, Durgabai Deshmukh, Hansa Mehta and Ammu Swaminathan).

It functioned both as a constitution-making body and as the Dominion Legislature (1947-1950). It adopted the National Flag (22 July 1947), the National Anthem and National Song (24 January 1950), and elected Rajendra Prasad as the first President. Critics said it was not representative (indirectly elected, dominated by the Congress and lawyers), but defenders note that it included diverse groups and debated extensively (the Constituent Assembly Debates run to about 12 volumes).
section-158: The Preamble indicates: (1) the source of authority - 'We, the people of India'; (2) the nature of the state - sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic, republic; (3) the objectives - justice (social, economic, political), liberty (of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship), equality (of status and opportunity) and fraternity (assuring the dignity of the individual and unity and integrity of the nation); and (4) the date of adoption - 26 November 1949.

The Preamble is based on Nehru's Objectives Resolution. It is not enforceable in courts, but it helps interpret the Constitution. In Kesavananda Bharati (1973), the Supreme Court held that the Preamble is part of the Constitution; in LIC of India (1995), the Court reaffirmed this. It has been amended once, by the 42nd Amendment (1976), adding 'socialist', 'secular' and 'integrity'; in 2024, the Supreme Court dismissed petitions challenging these additions.
section-159: Sovereignty means that India is a free and independent state, not subject to any external authority, with supreme power to make laws on any subject within its territory and to conduct its foreign policy independently. India became fully sovereign on 26 January 1950, when it ceased to be a British dominion.

India's membership of the Commonwealth (it remains a member, accepting the British monarch only as the symbolic 'head of the Commonwealth' under the London Declaration of 1949), the UN and other international organisations does not limit its sovereignty, because membership is voluntary. Sovereignty also means that India can acquire foreign territory or cede its territory (as in the Berubari case and the Land Boundary Agreement with Bangladesh, 100th Amendment, 2015).
section-160: 'Socialist' was added by the 42nd Amendment (1976), though socialist principles were already present in the Directive Principles. Indian socialism is 'democratic socialism', not communist or state socialism: it seeks to achieve socialist goals - reducing inequality, ending poverty and exploitation - through democratic and peaceful means, while allowing a mixed economy where public and private sectors coexist.

The Supreme Court in D. S. Nakara (1983) said the principal aim of a socialist state is to eliminate inequality in income, status and standards of life. Since the economic reforms of 1991 (liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation), the meaning of socialism in India has changed, but the commitment to social justice and welfare (subsidies, social security, employment guarantee, food security) continues.
section-161: 'Secular' was added by the 42nd Amendment (1976), but secularism was implicit in Articles 14, 15, 16 and 25-28 from the beginning. Indian secularism means: no state religion; equal respect for all religions; freedom of conscience and the right to profess, practise and propagate religion (Article 25); freedom of religious denominations to manage their affairs (Article 26); no tax for promoting a particular religion (Article 27); no religious instruction in state-funded schools (Article 28); and no discrimination on religious grounds.

Unlike the Western model of complete separation, Indian secularism allows the state to intervene to reform religious practices (such as abolishing untouchability, opening temples to all castes, and regulating religious institutions) and to support religious minorities' educational institutions (Article 30). In S. R. Bommai (1994), the Supreme Court held secularism to be part of the basic structure. Debates continue over issues such as personal laws, the Uniform Civil Code and the role of religion in politics.
section-162: Democratic means that the government derives its authority from the will of the people, expressed through periodic, free and fair elections based on universal adult franchise. India has a representative parliamentary democracy at the Union and state levels and democratic local self-government (panchayats and municipalities, 73rd and 74th Amendments, 1992). The term covers not only political democracy but also social and economic democracy.

Ambedkar, in his final speech to the Constituent Assembly (25 November 1949), emphasised that political democracy cannot last unless it rests on social democracy - a way of life recognising liberty, equality and fraternity. Democratic features of the Constitution include responsible government, an independent judiciary, rule of law, fundamental rights, a free press and accountability.
section-163: In a republic, the head of state is elected, not hereditary. In India, the President is elected indirectly for a fixed term of five years. A republic also means that political sovereignty is vested in the people, that public offices are open to all citizens without discrimination, and that there is no privileged class.

India is a 'democratic republic', unlike Britain, which is a 'democratic monarchy'. India became a republic on 26 January 1950. Although India remained a member of the Commonwealth, it accepted the British monarch only as the head of the Commonwealth, not as the head of the Indian state, under the London Declaration (1949).
section-164: Fundamental Rights are called 'fundamental' because they are guaranteed by the Constitution, are essential for the all-round development of individuals and are protected by the courts. They limit the power of the state (including Parliament, state legislatures, government and local authorities - Article 12) and provide the basis of democracy. They are inspired by the US Bill of Rights.

They can be enforced through the Supreme Court (Article 32) and High Courts (Article 226). They are subject to reasonable restrictions on grounds such as public order, morality, security of the state and sovereignty and integrity of India. Parliament can amend them but cannot destroy the basic structure (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973). During a national emergency, Article 19 rights are suspended automatically (in case of war or external aggression), and the President can suspend the enforcement of other rights except Articles 20 and 21.
section-165: Articles 14-18: Article 14 - equality before law (the British concept, a negative idea) and equal protection of laws (the American concept, a positive idea that equals should be treated equally and allows reasonable classification); Article 15 - prohibition of discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth, with special provisions for women, children, SCs, STs, socially and educationally backward classes (Article 15(4), added by the 1st Amendment, 1951) and economically weaker sections (Article 15(6), 103rd Amendment, 2019); Article 16 - equality of opportunity in public employment, allowing reservations (Article 16(4)).

Article 17 abolishes untouchability and forbids its practice in any form (the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955, and the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989, enforce it). Article 18 abolishes titles, except military and academic distinctions (the Supreme Court in Balaji Raghavan, 1996, held that national awards like Bharat Ratna and Padma awards are not titles). In Indra Sawhney (1992), the Supreme Court upheld OBC reservation but capped total reservation at 50 percent (with exceptions) and excluded the 'creamy layer'.
section-166: Articles 19-22: Article 19 guarantees six freedoms to citizens - (a) speech and expression (including the freedom of press, right to information and right to silence), (b) peaceful assembly without arms, (c) forming associations, unions and cooperative societies, (d) movement throughout India, (e) residence and settlement in any part of India, and (g) practising any profession, occupation, trade or business. (Clause (f) on property was deleted.) Reasonable restrictions can be imposed on grounds such as sovereignty and integrity, security of the state, public order, decency, morality, defamation and incitement to an offence.

Article 20 provides protection in respect of conviction for offences: no ex post facto criminal law, no double jeopardy and no self-incrimination. Article 21 - no person shall be deprived of life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law; it has been expanded to include the right to live with dignity, livelihood, privacy, health, education, environment, shelter, speedy trial, legal aid and the right to die with dignity (passive euthanasia, Common Cause, 2018). Article 21A (86th Amendment, 2002) - free and compulsory education for children aged 6 to 14. Article 22 - protection against arbitrary arrest and detention (right to be informed of grounds, to consult a lawyer, to be produced before a magistrate within 24 hours), and provisions on preventive detention.
section-167: Article 23 prohibits trafficking in human beings, begar (forced labour without payment) and other similar forms of forced labour; violation is punishable by law (the Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act, 1956, the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976). It applies to both the state and private individuals. However, the state can impose compulsory service for public purposes, such as military or social service, without discrimination.

Article 24 prohibits the employment of children below 14 years of age in factories, mines and other hazardous employment. Laws include the Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986, amended in 2016 to prohibit employment of children below 14 in all occupations (except family enterprises after school hours) and of adolescents (14-18) in hazardous occupations. The Supreme Court in M. C. Mehta v. State of Tamil Nadu (1996) directed the creation of a welfare fund for child labourers. In People's Union for Democratic Rights v. Union of India (1982, the Asiad workers case), the Court held that paying less than minimum wages amounts to forced labour.
section-168: Article 25 - all persons are equally entitled to freedom of conscience and the right to freely profess, practise and propagate religion, subject to public order, morality, health and other Fundamental Rights; the state can regulate secular activities associated with religious practice and provide for social welfare and reform, including throwing open Hindu religious institutions to all classes (Hindus include Sikhs, Jains and Buddhists for this purpose). Wearing and carrying kirpans by Sikhs is part of the profession of the Sikh religion.

Article 26 - religious denominations can establish and maintain institutions, manage their own affairs in matters of religion, and own and administer property. Article 27 - no person can be compelled to pay taxes for promoting any particular religion. Article 28 - no religious instruction in wholly state-funded educational institutions; in state-recognised or aided institutions, no one can be compelled to attend religious instruction. Courts use the 'essential religious practices' test to decide which practices are protected (for example, the Sabarimala case, 2018, and the triple talaq case, Shayara Bano, 2017).
section-169: Article 29 - any section of citizens having a distinct language, script or culture has the right to conserve it; and no citizen can be denied admission into state-maintained or aided educational institutions on grounds of religion, race, caste or language. Article 30 - all minorities, religious or linguistic, have the right to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice, and the state shall not discriminate in granting aid to such institutions.

The Supreme Court in T. M. A. Pai Foundation (2002) held that minority status is determined at the state level and that the state can regulate minority institutions to maintain standards but not interfere in their administration. Article 30 is meant to give minorities confidence and protect India's diversity. Mizoram's Christian-run schools and colleges are examples of institutions run by religious bodies, although in Mizoram Christians form the majority.
section-170: Article 32 gives the right to move the Supreme Court directly for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights. The Supreme Court can issue five writs: habeas corpus ('to have the body' - to produce a detained person and examine the legality of detention); mandamus ('we command' - directing a public official or body to perform a duty); prohibition (stopping a lower court from exceeding its jurisdiction); certiorari (quashing an order of a lower court or tribunal); and quo warranto ('by what authority' - inquiring into the legality of a person's claim to a public office).

Ambedkar called Article 32 'the very soul of the Constitution and the very heart of it'. High Courts can issue writs under Article 226 for Fundamental Rights and other legal rights, giving them wider writ jurisdiction. Article 32 is part of the basic structure and cannot be suspended except during an emergency (Article 359). Public Interest Litigation allows any public-spirited person to approach the court on behalf of those unable to do so.
section-171: Directive Principles (Part IV, Articles 36-51) are 'instruments of instructions' to the state, borrowed from the Irish Constitution. They aim to establish a welfare state and social and economic democracy. Examples: Article 39 (adequate means of livelihood, prevention of concentration of wealth, equal pay for equal work, protection of children); 39A (free legal aid, 42nd Amendment); 40 (village panchayats); 41 (right to work, education, public assistance); 43 (living wage); 43A (workers' participation in management); 44 (Uniform Civil Code); 45 (early childhood care and education, modified by the 86th Amendment); 46 (welfare of SCs, STs and weaker sections); 47 (nutrition, public health, prohibition); 48 (organisation of agriculture and animal husbandry); 48A (environment, forests and wildlife, 42nd Amendment); 49 (protection of monuments); 50 (separation of judiciary); 51 (international peace).

Many laws have implemented DPSPs: land reforms, the Minimum Wages Act, panchayati raj (73rd Amendment), the Right to Education Act (2009), the National Food Security Act (2013), MGNREGA (2005), legal aid (1987), environmental laws and prohibition in some states (including Mizoram). Conflicts between DPSP and Fundamental Rights were resolved through amendments (Articles 31A, 31B, 31C) and judicial decisions emphasising harmony (Minerva Mills, 1980).
section-172: There are eleven Fundamental Duties (Article 51A), added by the 42nd Amendment (1976) and the 86th Amendment (2002).
